articles.content:

articles.title: He Lost A Judgeship To A Blue Slip, His Comeback Made Double History
articles.content:
Ed. Note: Welcome to our daily feature Trivia Question of the Day!

Mississippi district attorney Scott Colom was blocked from a federal judgeship in 2023, when Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith refused to return her “blue slip” on his nomination. He responded by running against her — and won her Senate seat this month. Beyond unseating the senator who had blocked him, Colom’s victory gave his victory two noteworthy historic accomplishments. What were they?

Hint: One is a drought stretching back to 1982; while the other is a very first for Mississippi in the Senate.

See the answer on the next page.

The post He Lost A Judgeship To A Blue Slip, His Comeback Made Double History appeared first on Above the Law.

articles.title: Stat(s) Of The Week: An Uneasy Relationship
articles.content:
As AI becomes increasingly integrated into legal practice, concerns about its impact remain. “Trust but verify” describes many attorneys’ approach to AI use, according to a new report that also highlights their concerns about job security.
Half of the lawyers surveyed for Bloomberg Law’s AI in Practice report said they trust AI tools enough to use them for complex tasks, and more than 40% said they turn to AI to test legal arguments before asking colleagues.
At the same time, 92% of attorneys said they verify each citation and quotation that AI produces. Many lawyers, including 36% of associates and 22% of partners, said they spend more time correcting AI analysis than doing analytical tasks.
And then there are the fears of AI agents going rogue or replacing humans. Three out of four attorneys said they are at least somewhat concerned about AI agents acting outside their expected parameters. And more than a third of associates (36%) and even 16% of partners fear they will lose their jobs to AI.
State of Practice: Attorneys Rely on AI but Fear Losing Jobs [Bloomberg Law]
The post Stat(s) Of The Week: An Uneasy Relationship appeared first on Above the Law.

articles.title: AI In Our Courts: Useful Or A Magic 8 Ball?
articles.content:
AI is rearing its head in our courtrooms, and judges are having to decide what to make of it. Two recent decisions show a wrong way and a right way to do just that.
I recently wrote about a federal district court judge in Texas, Mark Pittman, who excoriated some attorneys because he thought they used AI to draft briefs. And because he didn’t like the arguments that they made. He labeled the lawyers lazy and called their arguments tortured. All before holding a hearing. It was my view that this was the wrong way to look at AI and those who use it.
Then along came an opinion out of the federal district court for the Eastern District of Kentucky. To me, it represents the right and studied way for courts to view AI and its use. The judge there denied a motion to dismiss by a cop who allegedly relied on AI facial recognition, and only AI, to make an arrest.
The cases are factually different. One involved lawyers using AI, the other a cop. But both turn on the same question: how should a court think about AI and its use by those appearing before it?
The Alleged Kentucky Facts
A Black man entered a bank in Florence, Ky., and attempted to cash what appeared to be a fraudulent check. The bank refused to cash the check, and he left. A security camera captured an unobstructed view of his face.
A local police department detective named Kilmer allegedly took a screenshot of the man’s face from the footage. He then used AI facial recognition technology to match that screenshot with a booking photo on file. The cop took the booking photo and a Facebook profile image he found and compared them to the screenshot. Voilà! He concluded they all matched and that a man named Osorio was the culprit.
This led Kilmer to sign a criminal complaint stating he had used “investigatory tools” to determine Osorio’s identity. He didn’t mention he used AI, by the way. An arrest warrant was ultimately issued and served on Osorio, a Nebraska resident, in Florida.
Osorio was then extradited to Kentucky, charged, and indicted even though he claimed the suspect in the footage looked nothing like him.
Eventually, the Kentucky prosecutors had to dismiss the indictment against Osorio with prejudice. Why? Because guess what, Osorio proved he was working in Nebraska when the fraudulent check was presented to the bank. Oops.
All this despite the fact that police department policy in that Kentucky jurisdiction stated that AI facial recognition technology was only advisory. And did not “establish probable cause without further investigation.”
Osorio didn’t take too kindly to being yanked out of Florida and brought to Kentucky for no good reason. So, he filed suit in federal district court against the cop. He is asserting claims for false arrest and imprisonment under the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments of the Constitution and Kentucky law, malicious prosecution, and assault and battery. The cop filed a motion to dismiss, arguing that qualified immunity shielded him from liability, among other things.
(Of course, for purposes of deciding a motion to dismiss, the court was required to take all Osorio’s allegations as true.)
The Motion To Dismiss
At the risk of oversimplifying, Judge S. Chad Meredith was presented with the issue of whether AI facial recognition technology alone could support a finding of probable cause and justify issuing a warrant. Like Pittman in Texas, Meredith faced the question of whether someone, this time a cop, had used AI appropriately.
But rather than attacking the cop, Meredith looked carefully at the law. He noted that qualified immunity could shield an officer from liability. But not if he violated a federal statutory or constitutional right, and the unlawfulness of his conduct was clearly established at the time of the violation.
And under the Fourth Amendment, neither probable cause nor a warrant can stand when based on materially false or misleading statements. Statements made knowingly or in reckless disregard for the truth.
The facts that the cop (a) delegated the entire task of determining probable cause to AI facial recognition technology without using any independent judgment on his part and (b) made misstatements or omissions in his affidavit to support the criminal complaint were sufficient, at this stage, to support the denial of the motion to dismiss.
Meredith posed an interesting hypothetical to support his findings:
Say that Detective Doe is called in to investigate a theft that occurred at a bank earlier in the day. As Detective Doe walks on the street in the vicinity of the bank, he uses a Magic 8 Ball to determine whether each pedestrian passerby is a potential suspect. The first pedestrian walks by, so Detective Doe shakes the Magic 8 Ball and asks whether that individual is the suspect: “My sources say no.” Then, Plaintiff Peter walks by, and Detective Doe once again shakes the Magic 8 Ball and asks whether Plaintiff Peter is the suspect: “You may rely on it.” Using the output from this “tool, “Detective Doe applies for a warrant to arrest Plaintiff Peter and states in his affidavit that he used “investigative tools” to match the suspect to Plaintiff Peter. Officers arrest Plaintiff Peter and he is charged with theft, but the charges are dropped and he is released when his alibi checks out.
The court noted that just because Plaintiff Peter couldn’t cite a case that using the Magic 8 Ball is a constitutional violation doesn’t mean relying on it was OK: “Any reasonable officer would know that additional investigative work is necessary to obtain sufficient probable cause for arrest; a Magic 8 Ball alone will not cut it.”
Judge Meredith concluded that while AI facial recognition technology has developed rapidly and is likely more reliable than the Magic 8 Ball, placing unquestioning reliance on it is still not much different. “No reasonable officer would think that Detective Kilmer’s allegedly exclusive reliance on AI is lawful — especially given how Osorio’s booking photograph looks nothing like the suspect from the security camera footage.”
Boom. Motion to Dismiss denied.
A Right Way To Think About AI
Meredith’s decision keeps AI in its rightful place. He refused to allow it to be used as the be-all, end-all. Indeed, without saying it outright, he confirmed the need to keep the proverbial human in the loop.
What the cop did was what many fear when it comes to AI. He simply relied on it too much and cut corners. Not to mention the fact that he appears to have been sneaky by saying he used “investigatory tools” to determine that Osorio was the guy. And sneaky is generous, given the police department’s explicit policy that AI alone could not establish probable cause. That didn’t help his cause.
The difference between how the Texas judge and the Kentucky judge looked at AI and its use could not be more stark. One simply blamed the lawyers for using AI in a case where the defendant’s liberty was at stake. The other carefully considered AI’s role in a civil proceeding arising from a criminal matter. And the cop’s use of AI without keeping a human in the loop. Meredith allowed a civil action to proceed where a person had been deprived of his liberty, even if only briefly, based on the law, not pique.
That’s a right and appropriate view of AI, not a knee-jerk reaction. Let’s hope more judges treat AI-related issues like Meredith and fewer like Pittman. Otherwise, we may all find ourselves behind the AI 8 Ball.
Stephen Embry is a lawyer, speaker, blogger, and writer. He publishes TechLaw Crossroads, a blog devoted to the examination of the tension between technology, the law, and the practice of law.
The post AI In Our Courts: Useful Or A Magic 8 Ball? appeared first on Above the Law.

articles.title: Many Lawyers Stopped Nickel-And-Diming Clients For Small Expenses
articles.content:
When I first started practicing law, attorneys at the law firm at which I worked needed to enter a billing code to complete many legal tasks. If an attorney wanted to make a telephone call, use the photocopier, or conduct legal research, the attorney needed to enter a client code so that the expense could be tracked and potentially passed along to the client. However, as technology has evolved and competition in the legal marketplace increased, many law firms have stopped charging clients separately for expenses that were once routinely included on legal bills.
One of the most obvious examples of this trend involves telephone charges. Decades ago, long-distance telephone calls could impose meaningful expenses on law firms, and it made some sense for firms to pass these costs along to clients. When I worked in Biglaw, attorneys needed to enter client codes when placing certain calls so that the firm could track the expense. However, most law firms now eat telephone charges rather than pass this cost onto clients, likely because law firms just pay flat rates for this service. Moreover, attorneys increasingly use cell phones and internet-based calling services to communicate with clients and other individuals involved in litigation. Under these circumstances, charging clients separately for routine telephone calls would seem strange, and many law firms no longer bother with such charges.
Photocopying expenses are another area in which law firms have changed their practices. Earlier in my career, attorneys and staff often needed to enter client codes when using photocopiers so that the firm could determine how many pages were copied for a particular matter. Some law firms charged clients a set amount per page, and these charges could add up, especially in cases involving substantial document productions. Photocopying involves paper, toner, and maintenance costs, and it is understandable that law firms historically sought to recover these amounts from clients.
However, much of the legal profession has moved away from paper documents, and attorneys now routinely exchange discovery materials, court filings, and correspondence electronically. Although some copying is still necessary, it is often easier for law firms to absorb routine photocopying costs as overhead rather than track every page and charge clients accordingly. Clients may also resent seeing relatively small copying charges on invoices, particularly when they are already paying substantial amounts for legal services. Of course, extraordinary copying or printing expenses may still justify separate charges, but routine photocopying is increasingly treated as part of the cost of doing business.
Legal research expenses have undergone a similar transformation. When I worked in Biglaw, attorneys often needed to enter client codes before conducting research on Westlaw or Lexis so that the firm could track the expense associated with a particular matter. Depending on the firm’s arrangement with the research provider, individual searches and other activities could generate charges that were passed along to clients. This sometimes created the awkward situation in which clients paid for an attorney’s time conducting research and then received an additional charge for the tools the attorney used to perform that research.
Nowadays, many law firms have flat-fee arrangements with legal research providers that allow attorneys to conduct substantial amounts of research without incurring additional per-search charges. Other firms use less expensive research platforms or free resources that make legal research far more affordable than it was in the past. As a result, some law firms no longer separately charge clients for routine legal research, even though these services still impose overhead expenses on the firm. In many situations, this approach makes sense since clients generally expect attorneys to have access to the tools necessary to perform their jobs.
There are also practical reasons why law firms have moved away from charging clients for relatively minor expenses. Tracking these charges requires administrative systems, staff time, and accounting procedures that may cost more than the amounts ultimately recovered. Attorneys and staff can waste time entering billing codes, correcting mistakes, and responding to questions about expenses that might only total a few dollars. Moreover, clients sometimes dispute these charges, which can create unnecessary friction in the attorney-client relationship.
Perhaps most importantly, law firms need to remain competitive in an increasingly crowded legal marketplace. Clients are more sophisticated about legal billing than ever before, and many compare the billing practices of different firms when deciding whom to retain. A client who is already paying hundreds of dollars per hour for legal services may reasonably wonder why a firm is also charging a few dollars for telephone calls, photocopies, or routine legal research. Even when these charges are technically justified, they can create the impression that a law firm is nickel-and-diming its clients.
Of course, law firms should still pass along substantial out-of-pocket expenses, such as filing fees, deposition transcripts, travel costs, and other charges that are directly attributable to a particular representation. However, there is a meaningful distinction between these expenses and the ordinary overhead costs associated with operating a modern law practice.
As technology continues to reduce the costs of performing routine legal tasks, more law firms should reconsider whether separately charging clients for minor expenses is worth the trouble. Sometimes, absorbing a relatively small cost can save administrative time, improve client relationships, and make a law firm more competitive. The legal profession has changed considerably since the days when attorneys needed a client code to make a telephone call, and law firm billing practices should reflect that reality.
Jordan Rothman is a partner of The Rothman Law Firm, a full-service New York and New Jersey law firm. He is also the founder of Student Debt Diaries, a website discussing how he paid off his student loans. You can reach Jordan through email at jordan@rothman.law.
